paras: The expulsion of Black strangers from Vincennes, Indiana, took place in July 1903, when city police were reported to be ordering all 'strange negroes' out of town after the Evansville race riot. The order was reported alongside the July 13 arrest of Henry Thomas, a Black man accused by a police commissioner of shouldering whites off a sidewalk. Only the Louisville Courier-Journal's correspondent reported the order directly, and Kentucky papers repeated it in short news notes.

In the days after the race riot at Evansville, Black residents who had left that city appeared in other Indiana towns, and correspondents at Vincennes wrote that many 'strange negroes' had arrived there. Both Vincennes dispatches claimed that some of the newcomers had taunted and insulted white people, and the Courier-Journal called them 'bold and desperate blacks.'

On the night of July 13, Sergeant McNell arrested Henry Thomas in the crowded business section on the complaint of George Gardner, a Democratic member of the board of police commissioners. Gardner said Thomas had elbowed him and others off the sidewalk and had jeered and cursed when they protested. Thomas, who was said to have arrived from Terre Haute that day and to have a wife in St. Louis, said he meant no harm and had apologized, which Gardner denied.

The arrest caused 'much excitement,' and to avoid the crowd officers took Thomas through City Hall and hurried him to jail. According to the Courier-Journal's special, the police were at the same time ordering all strange Black people out of Vincennes.
No report of a hearing for Thomas, of his release, or of how many people left the city under the order was found in the coverage.

The two Vincennes dispatches of July 14 told the story from the complainant's side: the Courier-Journal headed it 'Indiana City Aroused Over Alleged Impudence of a Black Man' and warned that 'serious trouble may be latent,' while the Indianapolis Journal ran it as 'Refugees Make Trouble.' The Courier-Journal printed the item beneath a report of a Booker T. Washington speech urging harmony between the races, and it alone carried the sentence about the order to leave.

Two days later the Crittenden Press of Marion, Kentucky, repeated the order and commented that the police were 'evidently going upon the theory that all strange negroes are bad negroes,' printing the paragraph twice in one issue. The Semi-Weekly Interior Journal of Stanford, Kentucky, wrote that Vincennes did not like being 'a haven of refuge' for Black people who had fled Evansville. No Black-press coverage of the Vincennes order or of Thomas's arrest was found.

Thomas and Gardner disagreed over whether Thomas had apologized, and both versions reached print only through the white dispatches. The Indianapolis Journal's dispatch described the newcomers but did not mention any order to leave, so the expulsion rests on the Courier-Journal's account.

bases: The only act of collective force reported is the Vincennes police ordering all 'strange negroes' out of town (A1, A3, A5); the arrest of Henry Thomas is the incident reported beside it (A1, A2).

The arrest of Henry Thomas is reported in two dispatches that agree (A1, A2), but the police order to leave appears only in the Courier-Journal special (A1) and in Kentucky news notes that repeat its sentence (A3, A5); the Indianapolis Journal dispatch does not mention it (A2).

accounts.label: Henry Thomas
accounts.gist: Thomas said he intended no harm and that he had apologized.

accounts.label: Vincennes correspondents
accounts.gist: Many Black people had come to Vincennes since the Evansville riot, some of whom insulted whites; the Courier-Journal's correspondent added that police were ordering all strange Black people out.

framing.detail: The Courier-Journal headed the special 'Indiana City Aroused Over Alleged Impudence of a Black Man' and described 'bold and desperate blacks' and 'arrogant' newcomers before reporting the order to leave.
The Indianapolis Journal headed its dispatch 'Refugees Make Trouble' and repeated that newcomers had 'taunted and thrown insults at whites'.
The Crittenden Press remarked that Vincennes police were 'evidently going upon the theory that all strange negroes are bad negroes,' contrasting this with a Kentucky town.
The Semi-Weekly Interior Journal summarized that Vincennes did not like being 'a haven of refuge' for Evansville refugees.
